atoms.title: Equivalence principle
atoms.summary: Locally, gravity and acceleration are indistinguishable — free fall is the closest thing to no force at all.

depths.eli5: Imagine you are in a windowless elevator and the cable snaps, so you and the elevator fall together. While you fall, you float in the middle of the elevator — nothing pushes on you, exactly like an astronaut drifting in empty space far from any planet. The big idea: while you are falling freely, you cannot feel gravity at all. Falling and floating-in-empty-space feel identical from the inside.
depths.core: A 'gravitational field' is the region around a mass where gravity acts; a 'frame' (reference frame) is just the viewpoint of a particular observer, like 'the elevator's point of view.' Einstein noticed that, in a small enough region, the pull of a uniform gravitational field feels exactly the same as being inside an accelerating rocket, and a freely falling viewpoint feels exactly like having no gravity at all. The reason every object falls the same way is that two kinds of mass are equal: inertial mass (how hard it is to push an object into motion) and gravitational mass (how strongly gravity grabs it). Because these are equal to extreme precision, a feather and a hammer fall identically in a vacuum. This lets us stop treating gravity as a force and start treating it as a feature of the viewpoint you choose.
depths.deep: The equality of inertial and gravitational mass is the empirical seed; the principle is only exactly true locally (in a small enough region), because real gravity has tidal effects — neighboring free-fall paths converge, and that convergence is curvature, which cannot be transformed away.

atoms.note: The 'happiest thought of my life' — Einstein, on realizing a falling person feels no weight.

quiz.answer: Inertial mass (resistance to acceleration) and gravitational mass (the 'charge' that responds to gravity).

quiz.answer: Real gravity has tidal effects: over an extended region, free-fall paths converge or diverge, revealing curvature that no single accelerating frame can mimic.

atoms.title: Spacetime curvature
atoms.summary: Gravity is not a force pulling through space — it is the geometry of spacetime being curved by energy.

depths.eli5: Picture a stretchy trampoline. Put a bowling ball in the middle and the surface sags. Now roll a marble nearby and it curves toward the ball — not because the ball reaches out and grabs it, but because the surface itself is bent. Gravity works like that. 'Spacetime' is the combination of the three directions of space plus time, treated as one stretchy fabric. Heavy things bend that fabric, and everything else just coasts along the bends. Earth doesn't tug the Moon with an invisible rope; Earth bends the spacetime around it, and the Moon rolls along the curve.
depths.core: In general relativity (Einstein's theory of gravity), matter and energy curve four-dimensional spacetime, and that curvature tells matter how to move. 'Four-dimensional' just means three space directions plus time. What we feel as gravitational attraction is objects following the straightest available path through a curved geometry — the same way a plane flying 'straight' over the curved Earth traces a curved arc on a flat map. Curvature is detectable in a small region only through tidal effects: the slow relative drift of two nearby objects that are both falling freely. That drift is the un-fakeable fingerprint of real gravity.
depths.deep: Curvature is encoded in the Riemann tensor, which measures the failure of a vector to return to itself after parallel transport around a closed loop; it cannot be removed by any change of coordinates, unlike the apparent 'force' of gravity in a single frame.

atoms.art_prompt: a rubber-sheet grid dimpled by a massive sphere, with a smaller body coasting along the curved gridlines

quiz.prompt: In general relativity, what plays the role that 'gravitational force' played in Newton's picture?
quiz.answer: The curvature of spacetime — matter follows curved geometry rather than being pulled by a force.

quiz.prompt: Explain to a beginner why a single observer in free fall can't detect gravity but tidal forces still reveal it.
quiz.answer: Free fall cancels the uniform part of gravity locally, so you float. But two nearby falling objects drift relative to each other because of curvature — that residual relative acceleration (tidal effect) is the true, un-removable signature of gravity.

atoms.title: The metric and spacetime intervals
atoms.summary: The metric tensor measures distances and times in spacetime; it is the field that encodes gravity.

depths.eli5: Think of a map where the grid lines are not evenly spaced — in some places the squares are stretched, in others squished. To find the real distance between two dots you can't just count squares; you need a rule that says how much real distance each square is worth at that spot. The metric is exactly that rule. It's a ruler that changes from place to place, and it tells you how far apart two points really are once space is bent.
depths.core: The 'metric tensor,' written g (with two small indices, g_{μν}), is the master rulebook of geometry. A 'tensor' is just an organized table of numbers that behaves correctly when you switch viewpoints. The metric takes the raw difference in coordinates between two nearby points (dx) and turns it into the real physical separation, written ds (the 'interval'). The equation ds² = g_{μν} dx^μ dx^ν is shorthand for 'sum up the coordinate steps, each weighted by the metric, to get the true squared distance.' In flat, gravity-free spacetime the metric is the simple fixed 'Minkowski metric.' In curved spacetime it varies from point to point — and that variation IS gravity. Every geometric thing — lengths, times, angles, and ultimately curvature — is computed from the metric and how it changes.
depths.deep: The interval ds² is invariant under coordinate changes, which is what makes physics observer-independent; the metric's second derivatives build the Riemann curvature, so g_{μν} is simultaneously the 'ruler' and the gravitational potential of general relativity.

atoms.art_prompt: a warped coordinate grid where the spacing of gridlines stretches and compresses near a mass, with a tiny ruler measuring a curved interval

quiz.prompt: What does the metric tensor g_{μν} let you compute from coordinate differences?
quiz.answer: Physical spacetime intervals ds — actual distances and proper times — including how they bend in curved spacetime.

quiz.prompt: Why is the invariance of ds² important for physics?
quiz.answer: Because ds² is the same for all observers regardless of coordinates, it guarantees that physical predictions don't depend on the arbitrary coordinate system chosen.

atoms.title: Geodesics — free-fall paths
atoms.summary: Free-falling bodies follow geodesics — the straightest possible paths through curved spacetime.

depths.eli5: On a flat floor the shortest path between two points is a straight line. But on a globe, the 'straightest' path you can walk — a great-circle route, like the arc a long-distance flight follows — looks curved on a flat map. In bent spacetime it's the same: a freely coasting object always takes the locally straightest route available, and because spacetime is curved that route looks like a curve. That's why a thrown ball arcs and why planets loop around the Sun — they're going as straight as the curved geometry allows.
depths.core: A 'geodesic' is the generalization of a straight line to curved spacetime: the path an object follows when nothing but gravity acts on it (no engines, no friction, no push). Technically it 'extremizes proper time' — proper time is the time measured by a clock carried along the path, and a free-falling object travels the route that makes its own clock tick the most. The equation has two parts: the first term (d²x/dτ²) is the path's acceleration as you move along it, and the second term contains the 'Christoffel symbols' (the Γ symbols). The Christoffel symbols are bookkeeping numbers, built from how the metric changes from place to place, that tell you how the direction 'straight ahead' twists as you move through bent space. Setting the whole thing to zero says: 'go straight ahead, correcting only for the bending of the space itself.'
depths.deep: Massive particles follow timelike geodesics (maximizing proper time — the 'twin paradox' resolution), light follows null geodesics; the deviation of neighboring geodesics is governed by the Riemann tensor, directly linking free fall to curvature.

quiz.prompt: What kind of path does an object in free fall follow in general relativity?
quiz.answer: A geodesic — the straightest possible (proper-time-extremizing) path through curved spacetime.

quiz.answer: Massive particles follow timelike geodesics (nonzero proper time, maximized), while light follows null geodesics where ds² = 0.

atoms.title: Stress-energy tensor
atoms.summary: The stress-energy tensor packages all energy, momentum, pressure, and stress — it is the source of gravity.

depths.eli5: Newton thought only 'how much stuff' (mass) makes gravity. Einstein found that more things matter: not just mass, but energy, motion, and even pressure all bend spacetime. The stress-energy tensor is a tidy table that lists all of that 'stuff' at every point in space. It's the complete inventory of what gravity responds to.
depths.core: The stress-energy tensor, written T_{μν}, is a 4-by-4 table (a tensor — an organized grid of numbers that switches viewpoints correctly) that records, at every point, the density and flow of energy and momentum. 'Density' means how much per unit volume; 'flux' means how much is flowing through a surface; 'momentum' is mass times velocity, the measure of motion. The top-left entry is energy density (how much energy is packed into each bit of space, and via E=mc² that includes mass). Other entries hold momentum flow and pressure/stress (the push matter exerts sideways and outward). The key surprise of general relativity: gravity is sourced by this entire table, not by mass alone. Because pressure is included, radiation (light, which has pressure but no rest mass) and 'dark energy' (which has large negative pressure) bend spacetime differently from ordinary slow-moving matter ('dust').
depths.deep: Local conservation of energy-momentum, ∇_μ T^{μν} = 0, follows automatically from the field equations via the Bianchi identities — energy conservation is geometrically built in, not imposed.

atoms.art_prompt: a 4x4 grid of cells labeled energy density, momentum flux, and pressure, glowing as the source feeding a curved-spacetime backdrop

quiz.prompt: Beyond mass density, what other quantity does the stress-energy tensor include that also gravitates?
quiz.answer: Pressure (and momentum/stress) — which is why radiation and dark energy gravitate differently from ordinary matter.

quiz.prompt: What physical law is automatically encoded in ∇_μ T^{μν} = 0?
quiz.answer: Local conservation of energy and momentum, which follows geometrically from the field equations.

atoms.title: Einstein field equations
atoms.summary: Matter and energy curve spacetime; spacetime curvature tells matter how to move — in one tensor equation.

depths.eli5: This is the single rule at the heart of Einstein's gravity, and it's a two-way street: stuff bends space, and bent space steers stuff. The physicist John Wheeler put it best — 'matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime tells matter how to move.' Everything else in this whole branch is working out the consequences of this one balanced statement.
depths.core: Read the equation as a balance with geometry on the left and contents on the right. The left side has the 'Einstein tensor' G_{μν} — a specific recipe built from spacetime's curvature — so the left side describes the shape of spacetime. The right side has the stress-energy tensor T_{μν} (the inventory of energy, momentum, and pressure from the previous atom), so the right side describes what's filling spacetime. The number out front, 8πG/c⁴, is just a conversion factor (G is Newton's gravitational constant, c is the speed of light) chosen so that in everyday weak, slow situations the equation reproduces Newton's familiar gravity. The extra Λ g_{μν} term is the optional 'cosmological constant' Λ, which behaves like a built-in energy of empty space and becomes important on cosmic scales. So: curvature on the left = matter-and-energy on the right.
depths.deep: These are ten coupled nonlinear partial differential equations; their nonlinearity (gravity gravitates) is why exact solutions are rare and precious — Schwarzschild, Kerr, and the FRW cosmologies are among the few. Λ originally added to permit a static universe, later revived as dark energy.

atoms.note: Λ was Einstein's 'biggest blunder' (his words) — added then removed, then resurrected by the 1998 acceleration discovery.
atoms.art_prompt: a balanced equation with a glowing curved-grid geometry on the left and a luminous matter-energy cloud on the right, joined by the constant 8πG/c⁴

quiz.prompt: In the Einstein field equations, which side describes geometry and which describes matter?
quiz.answer: The Einstein tensor side (G_{μν} + Λg_{μν}) describes spacetime geometry; the stress-energy side (T_{μν}) describes matter and energy.

quiz.prompt: Summarize the physical meaning of the field equations in one sentence a student can remember.
quiz.answer: Matter and energy tell spacetime how to curve, and the curvature of spacetime tells matter how to move.

atoms.title: Cosmological principle
atoms.summary: On large enough scales the universe is homogeneous and isotropic — the same everywhere and in every direction.

depths.eli5: Up close the universe is lumpy — planets here, empty gaps there. But zoom way out, past individual galaxies, and the lumps blur into an even haze that looks the same no matter where you're standing or which direction you look. There's no center of the universe and no edge you could point to, and no special direction that's different from the rest.
depths.core: The cosmological principle is the starting assumption of modern cosmology. It says that, once you average over enormous distances (hundreds of millions of light-years — a light-year is the distance light travels in a year), the universe is 'homogeneous' (the same at every location, no special spot) and 'isotropic' (the same in every direction, no special way to point). These two symmetries are an enormous simplification: they let cosmologists shrink Einstein's ten complicated field equations down to just a couple of equations describing a single number, the 'scale factor,' that captures the whole large-scale universe. It's an idealization — locally the universe is very lumpy — but on the largest scales the evidence backs it up.
depths.deep: It is an idealization that holds statistically on large scales — galaxies cluster strongly on small scales, but the CMB's near-perfect uniformity (~1 part in 100,000) is the strongest observational support for large-scale isotropy around us.

atoms.art_prompt: a deep field of galaxies that looks statistically identical inside several boxes placed at different positions and orientations

quiz.prompt: Name the two symmetry assumptions of the cosmological principle.
quiz.answer: Homogeneity (same at every location) and isotropy (same in every direction) on large scales.

quiz.prompt: What is the strongest observational evidence for large-scale isotropy?
quiz.answer: The cosmic microwave background's near-perfect uniformity across the sky (anisotropies of only ~1 part in 100,000).

atoms.title: FRW metric
atoms.summary: The unique metric of a homogeneous, isotropic universe — flat, open, or closed, all scaled by a(t).

depths.eli5: Once you assume the universe looks the same everywhere and in every direction, its shape gets incredibly simple to describe: just one stretchy number, written a(t), that says how big everything is at time t, plus a single choice of overall shape — flat like a tabletop, curved-closed like the surface of a ball, or curved-open like a saddle. This metric is that description boiled down to its essentials.
depths.core: The FRW metric (Friedmann–Robertson–Walker, sometimes FLRW with Lemaître's name added) is the unique shape the metric must take once you accept the cosmological principle. Reading the equation: −c²dt² is the time part (c is the speed of light, t is time), and the bracket is the space part. The 'curvature constant' k labels which of three uniform spatial shapes you have: k = +1 is 'closed' (finite, ball-like), k = 0 is 'flat' (the everyday geometry where parallel lines stay parallel), and k = −1 is 'open' (infinite, saddle-like). The function a(t), the 'scale factor,' multiplies every spatial distance and grows over time — that growth is the expansion of the universe. 't' here is 'cosmic time,' the time read by clocks moving along with the average flow of matter.
depths.deep: The coordinates are comoving: galaxies sit at fixed (r, θ, φ) while a(t) stretches the physical distances between them. Observations strongly favor k ≈ 0 (spatially flat) to within current measurement error.

atoms.art_prompt: three model universes side by side — flat sheet, sphere, saddle — each filled with a comoving galaxy grid stretching uniformly over time

quiz.prompt: What does the curvature constant k = +1, 0, −1 represent in the FRW metric?
quiz.answer: The three possible uniform spatial geometries: closed (k=+1), flat (k=0), and open (k=−1).

quiz.prompt: In comoving coordinates, why don't galaxies' coordinates change as the universe expands?
quiz.answer: Galaxies sit at fixed comoving coordinates; it is the scale factor a(t) multiplying those coordinates that stretches the physical distances between them.

atoms.title: Scale factor a(t)
atoms.summary: A single function a(t) sets the size of the universe; its growth is cosmic expansion.

depths.eli5: Draw galaxies as dots on the surface of a balloon, then blow the balloon up. Every dot drifts away from every other dot, even though no dot is the 'center.' The scale factor, written a(t), is basically 'how inflated the balloon is at time t.' When a doubles, every distance between dots doubles.
depths.core: The scale factor a(t) is a single number, changing with time t, that tracks how stretched-out the universe is. By convention it's set to exactly 1 right now, so today's value is a(t₀) = 1 (t₀ means 'today'). The distance between any two 'comoving' objects — objects just drifting along with the overall expansion, not zooming around on their own — scales in proportion to a(t): if a was 1/2 in the past, all those distances were half as big then. Because everything large-scale rides on this one number, the history of the universe is essentially the story of how a(t) grows. Its rate of change (first derivative, written ȧ) is the expansion speed, and the rate of change of that (second derivative) says whether the expansion is speeding up or slowing down. The word 'derivative' just means 'how fast something is changing.'
depths.deep: a(t) is dimensionless with the convention a(t₀)=1; redshift, temperature, and density all map directly onto it (1+z = 1/a), making a(t) the master clock of cosmic history even though it is not directly observable — only ratios are.

quiz.prompt: What is the value of the scale factor today, by convention?
quiz.answer: a(t₀) = 1; earlier times have a < 1 and the future has a > 1 in an expanding universe.

quiz.prompt: If the scale factor was a = 0.5 at some past epoch, how do physical distances then compare to today?
quiz.answer: All distances between comoving objects were half their present values.

atoms.title: Cosmological redshift
atoms.summary: Expansion stretches light's wavelength as it travels — distant galaxies look redder by exactly the factor space has grown.

depths.eli5: Light travels as waves, and the color you see depends on the wave's length — shorter waves look bluer, longer waves look redder. Draw a wave on a rubber band, then stretch the band: the wave gets longer. As the universe grows, it stretches the light waves crossing it the same way, making them longer and therefore redder. So light from very distant galaxies, which spent a long time crossing growing space, arrives shifted toward red. That shift is called 'redshift.'
depths.core: A 'photon' is a single particle of light, and its 'wavelength' is the length of one wave. As a photon crosses expanding space, its wavelength stretches in exact proportion to the scale factor a(t). 'Redshift' z is the fractional amount the wavelength grew: the formula 1 + z = λ_observed / λ_emitted = 1 / a(t_emit) says the stretch factor equals one over the scale factor at the moment the light left (t_emit). So measuring a galaxy's redshift directly tells you how small the universe was when its light departed. Important subtlety: this is NOT the everyday 'Doppler shift' you hear when a siren passes (caused by something moving through space). Cosmological redshift comes from space itself stretching while the light is in flight.
depths.deep: Distinguishing cosmological redshift from peculiar-velocity Doppler shifts matters near home; at high z the relation 1+z=1/a is exact within FRW and is how we read the scale factor off the spectrum of any source — redshift is our primary cosmic distance/time coordinate.

quiz.prompt: What does a galaxy's redshift z directly tell you about the scale factor when its light was emitted?
quiz.answer: 1 + z = 1/a(t_emit), so a higher z means the light left when the universe was smaller.

quiz.prompt: A galaxy is observed at z = 1. By what factor has the universe expanded since the light left?
quiz.answer: By a factor of 2, since a(t_emit) = 1/(1+z) = 1/2.

atoms.title: Hubble–Lemaître law
atoms.summary: Galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance — the observational signature of cosmic expansion.

depths.eli5: When astronomers measure how fast galaxies are moving away from us, they find a clean pattern: a galaxy twice as far away is moving away twice as fast. That's exactly what you'd see if the whole of space were quietly growing everywhere at once — and it's the everyday evidence that the universe is expanding.
depths.core: 'Recession velocity' is how fast a galaxy moves away from us. The Hubble–Lemaître law says this velocity v is simply proportional to the galaxy's distance d: v = H₀ d. The proportionality number H₀ is the 'Hubble constant,' about 70 km/s per megaparsec today (a megaparsec, Mpc, is about 3.26 million light-years; the units mean a galaxy gains ~70 km/s of recession for every Mpc of distance). This doesn't mean we sit at a center — in a uniformly expanding universe every observer sees the same law. The broader 'Hubble parameter' H = ȧ/a is the fractional growth rate of the scale factor (ȧ is how fast a is changing, divided by a itself), and its present value H₀ roughly sets both the age and the size scale of the universe.
depths.deep: 1/H₀ is the Hubble time (~14 billion years), a first estimate of the age; the law is exact only at low z, where v ≈ cz — at high z one must use the full FRW relation between redshift and distance rather than a naive velocity.

atoms.note: Renamed Hubble–Lemaître law in 2018 to credit Lemaître's 1927 derivation.
atoms.art_prompt: a scatter plot of galaxy recession velocity versus distance forming a straight line through the origin, slope labeled H_0

quiz.prompt: What does the Hubble constant H₀ relate, and roughly what is its value?
quiz.answer: It relates a galaxy's recession velocity to its distance (v = H₀d), with H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc.

quiz.prompt: Show why 1/H₀ gives a rough age of the universe.
quiz.answer: If expansion had been at a constant rate, a galaxy at distance d receding at v = H₀d took time d/v = 1/H₀ to get there; 1/H₀ ≈ 14 Gyr is therefore a first estimate of the age.

atoms.title: Friedmann equations
atoms.summary: The Einstein equations applied to a uniform universe — they govern how the scale factor evolves.

depths.eli5: This is the universe's growth equation. Tell it what the universe is made of right now — ordinary matter, radiation (light), its overall shape, and dark energy — and it tells you how fast the universe is growing and whether that growth is speeding up or slowing down. It's the master equation of cosmology.
depths.core: When you feed the simple FRW shape of the universe into Einstein's field equations, all that machinery collapses into the much friendlier Friedmann equations. The one shown gives H², the square of the expansion rate (H = ȧ/a, the fractional growth rate from the Hubble-law atom). On the right: ρ (Greek 'rho') is the total energy density — how much energy-and-matter is packed into each bit of space; the −kc²/a² term carries the universe's curvature k (its overall shape); and the Λ term is dark energy. A companion 'acceleration' equation shows that pressure, not just density, decides whether expansion speeds up or slows down. The key plot twist: the different ingredients thin out at different rates as the universe grows, so each one takes its turn dominating the cosmic story.
depths.deep: Matter density scales as a⁻³, radiation as a⁻⁴ (extra factor from redshift), curvature as a⁻², and Λ stays constant — so the universe passes through radiation-, matter-, and Λ-dominated eras as a grows, with a(t)∝t^{1/2}, t^{2/3}, and e^{Ht} respectively.

quiz.prompt: What does the first Friedmann equation give in terms of the universe's contents?
quiz.answer: The expansion rate H² = (ȧ/a)² in terms of energy density, spatial curvature, and the cosmological constant.

quiz.prompt: Why does radiation density fall as a⁻⁴ while matter falls as a⁻³?
quiz.answer: Both dilute by volume (a⁻³); radiation gets one extra factor of a⁻¹ because each photon's wavelength stretches with expansion, lowering its energy.

atoms.title: Critical density and Ω
atoms.summary: The density that makes space exactly flat; Ω compares the actual density to it and fixes the geometry.

depths.eli5: There's one special amount of stuff that makes the universe come out perfectly flat — like a tabletop, where parallel lines stay parallel forever. Pack in more than that special amount and space curves around on itself like the surface of a ball; pack in less and it curves the other way like a saddle. Measuring how much stuff the universe actually has tells you which shape we live in.
depths.core: Take the Friedmann equation and ask: what energy density would make the curvature term k vanish, giving a perfectly flat universe? That special value is the 'critical density,' ρ_c = 3H²/(8πG), where H is the expansion rate and G is Newton's gravitational constant. Now compare the real density ρ to this critical value: the ratio Ω = ρ/ρ_c (Greek capital 'Omega') is the 'density parameter,' and it fixes the geometry. Ω > 1 means denser than critical → space is closed and curves like a ball; Ω = 1 means exactly critical → space is flat; Ω < 1 means underdense → space is open and saddle-shaped. When you add up Ω from every ingredient — ordinary matter, radiation, and dark energy — observations land remarkably close to a total of 1, meaning the universe is flat.
depths.deep: The sum Ω_m + Ω_r + Ω_Λ + Ω_k = 1 is an identity, so 'flatness' (Ω_k ≈ 0) is the measured statement that the energy components add to the critical density to within ~0.5% — a result inflation predicts and the CMB confirms.

quiz.prompt: What value of Ω corresponds to a spatially flat universe?
quiz.answer: Ω = 1, where the actual density equals the critical density ρ_c = 3H²/8πG.

quiz.prompt: If Ω_m ≈ 0.31 and Ω_Λ ≈ 0.69 with negligible radiation, what does this say about spatial curvature?
quiz.answer: They sum to ≈ 1.0, so Ω_k ≈ 0 — the universe is spatially flat to within measurement error.

atoms.title: The Big Bang — a hot dense beginning
atoms.summary: Run the expansion backward and the universe was hotter, denser, and smaller — the Big Bang is that hot early state.

depths.eli5: Play the movie of the expanding universe backwards. Everything that is flying apart today was packed closer and closer together the further back you go — and packing things tightly together makes them hot (squeeze any gas and it heats up). So long ago the whole universe was tiny, dense, and blazing hot. That hot, tiny early state is what 'the Big Bang' means. It was NOT an explosion that went off at one spot in empty space — it was the entire universe starting out small and hot everywhere at once.
depths.core: The Big Bang is the name for the early, hot, dense phase of the universe, back when the scale factor a(t) was tiny. As a grew, the universe cooled and thinned out ('rarefied'). The model rests on three independent pillars of evidence that all point to the same hot dense origin roughly 13.8 billion years ago: (1) the observed expansion of the universe (galaxies flying apart, the Hubble law); (2) the cosmic microwave background, a faint glow of leftover heat filling the whole sky; and (3) the measured amounts of the lightest chemical elements (hydrogen, helium), which match what a hot early furnace would have produced. A common misconception worth deleting: there is no center and no edge — space itself expanded everywhere, not stuff blasting outward into a pre-existing void.
depths.deep: Extrapolating a → 0 gives a formal singularity of infinite density, but that is a breakdown of classical general relativity, not a verified physical event — the earliest moments require quantum gravity, and the standard hot Big Bang is only confidently described from roughly a microsecond onward.

atoms.note: The age 13.8 Gyr comes from fitting the expansion history (CMB + supernovae + large-scale structure).

quiz.answer: It was not matter blasting outward into pre-existing space; it was the hot, dense early state of space itself expanding everywhere at once — there is no center and no edge.

atoms.title: Thermal history and temperature scaling
atoms.summary: The universe cools as it expands; its temperature is inversely proportional to the scale factor.

depths.eli5: Letting a gas expand cools it down — it's why an aerosol can feels cold as it sprays. The universe does the same thing as it grows: it cools, and in a beautifully simple way. Make the universe twice as big and its temperature drops to half. So the early, tiny universe was scorching, and it has been cooling ever since.
depths.core: Temperature, written T, measures how hot something is (here in kelvin, K, the science temperature scale starting from absolute zero). Because the universe is bathed in light whose wavelengths stretch as the scale factor a grows, the temperature of that cosmic radiation falls in lockstep: T ∝ 1/a, which equals 1 + z (the redshift). This one relation turns the scale factor into a cosmic thermometer — each chapter of history happened at a characteristic temperature: light-element formation at about a billion kelvin (10⁹ K), atoms forming at about 3000 K, and the leftover glow we see today at just 2.725 K. So 'how hot was the universe then?' and 'how big was it then?' are the same question.
depths.deep: The scaling is exact for a thermal blackbody spectrum, which expansion preserves: a redshifted blackbody is still a blackbody at lower temperature — the reason the CMB remains a near-perfect Planck spectrum despite stretching by a factor of ~1100.

quiz.answer: T ∝ 1/a = 1 + z — the universe cools as it expands.

quiz.answer: About 2.725 × 1101 ≈ 3000 K, the temperature at which neutral hydrogen formed.

atoms.title: Cosmic inflation
atoms.summary: A burst of exponential expansion in the first instant explains the universe's flatness, uniformity, and seed fluctuations.

depths.eli5: In the first sliver of a second after the Big Bang, the universe is thought to have ballooned in size by a staggering amount almost instantly. Think of a wrinkled balloon blown up so fast that any wrinkle gets stretched flat and smooth. That sudden growth smoothed the universe out, flattened its shape, and stretched microscopic jitters into the faint lumps that would later grow into galaxies.
depths.core: Inflation is the idea that the very early universe went through a brief burst of runaway expansion — the size grew exponentially, a ∝ e^{Ht} (e is the natural growth constant; H sets the breakneck rate). The proposed engine is a 'scalar field,' a kind of energy spread evenly through space whose stored ('potential') energy temporarily acts like powerful anti-gravity. Inflation was invented to fix two puzzles in the plain Big Bang: the 'horizon problem' (why regions on opposite sides of the sky have the same temperature even though, without inflation, they were never close enough to swap heat) and the 'flatness problem' (why the density parameter Ω is so suspiciously close to 1). Both are solved if a tiny patch that WAS in contact got stretched to cover the entire visible universe. As a bonus, tiny quantum jitters (unavoidable random fluctuations at microscopic scales) got stretched to cosmic size and became the seeds from which all galaxies grew.
depths.deep: Inflation's most testable prediction is a nearly scale-invariant spectrum of adiabatic, Gaussian density perturbations with slight red tilt (n_s ≈ 0.965) — confirmed by the CMB; a primordial gravitational-wave (B-mode) signal would be smoking-gun evidence but has not yet been detected.

atoms.note: Proposed by Guth (1980) and refined by Linde, Albrecht, and Steinhardt.

atoms.art_prompt: a tiny smooth patch exploding in size by a vast factor in a sliver of time, with quantum ripples on it being stretched to cosmic scale

quiz.prompt: Name two long-standing puzzles that inflation was designed to solve.
quiz.answer: The horizon problem (large-scale uniformity) and the flatness problem (Ω ≈ 1).

quiz.prompt: How does inflation explain why widely separated parts of the sky have the same CMB temperature?
quiz.answer: They were in causal contact in a tiny pre-inflation patch that inflation then stretched across the whole observable universe, so they share a common thermal history.

atoms.title: Baryogenesis
atoms.summary: Some unknown process produced slightly more matter than antimatter, leaving the matter we see today.

depths.eli5: Every particle of matter has a mirror-image 'antimatter' twin, and when a particle meets its twin they wipe each other out in a flash of light. In the hot early universe there was nearly as much antimatter as matter, so almost everything annihilated. But for every billion-and-one bits of matter there were only a billion bits of antimatter — a tiny imbalance. After all the pairs cancelled, that leftover one-in-a-billion sliver of matter is everything we see: every star, planet, and person.
depths.core: 'Antimatter' is a counterpart to ordinary matter with opposite electric charge; when a particle meets its antiparticle they 'annihilate,' converting into radiation. A 'baryon' is a heavy particle like a proton or neutron — the building blocks of atomic nuclei. If matter and antimatter had been made in exactly equal amounts, they'd have annihilated completely and left a universe of pure light with no atoms. Instead a tiny surplus of matter — about one extra baryon for every billion photons of light — survived. Producing that surplus requires three ingredients spelled out by physicist Andrei Sakharov: (1) baryon number must not be perfectly conserved (so the count of baryons can change), (2) there must be 'C and CP violation' (a built-in lopsidedness so matter and antimatter aren't treated identically), and (3) the universe must fall out of perfect thermal balance ('equilibrium') at the right moment.
depths.deep: The Standard Model contains all three Sakharov ingredients in principle but provides far too little CP violation and too weak a departure from equilibrium to explain the observed baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6×10⁻¹⁰ — so baryogenesis is strong evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how large was the matter–antimatter asymmetry that survived?
quiz.answer: About one extra baryon per billion photons (baryon-to-photon ratio η ≈ 6×10⁻¹⁰).

quiz.prompt: Why is baryogenesis considered evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model?
quiz.answer: The Standard Model's CP violation and out-of-equilibrium dynamics are far too weak to produce the observed asymmetry, so new physics is required.

atoms.title: Big Bang nucleosynthesis
atoms.summary: In the first few minutes the universe forged the light elements; their measured abundances match the prediction precisely.

depths.eli5: When the universe was just a few minutes old it was hot and dense enough to act like a giant nuclear furnace, cooking the simplest atomic nuclei — mostly hydrogen and helium. Here's the amazing part: when astronomers measure how much hydrogen and helium the universe actually has today, the amounts match what this few-minute furnace should have made. That agreement is one of the strongest reasons to trust the Big Bang picture.
depths.core: 'Nucleosynthesis' means building atomic nuclei. A nucleus is the dense core of an atom, made of protons and neutrons. 'Nuclear fusion' is when small nuclei stick together to form bigger ones, releasing energy. Between about one second and a few minutes after the Big Bang, the universe was hot and dense enough for fusion to run. Protons and neutrons fused into 'deuterium' (a heavy form of hydrogen), then mostly into 'helium-4' (about 25% of all ordinary matter by weight), plus a trace of 'lithium-7' — and essentially nothing heavier (those came much later inside stars). How much of each formed depends sensitively on the 'baryon-to-photon ratio' (how many ordinary matter particles there were per particle of light). The predicted amounts match the measured ones beautifully — a landmark success of cosmology.
depths.deep: Deuterium is the most sensitive 'baryometer': its abundance pins the baryon density independently of the CMB, and the two agree, strongly constraining how much ordinary (baryonic) matter exists — far less than the total matter, which is why most matter must be non-baryonic.

quiz.answer: About 25% of ordinary (baryonic) matter by mass, with the rest mostly hydrogen and traces of deuterium and lithium.

quiz.prompt: Why does BBN, combined with the total matter density, imply non-baryonic dark matter?
quiz.answer: BBN fixes the baryon density (via deuterium especially) at a value far below the total matter density inferred from gravity, so most matter cannot be baryons.

atoms.title: Recombination and last scattering
atoms.summary: At ~380,000 years the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, releasing the light we now see as the CMB.

depths.eli5: Imagine thick fog: light can't travel far because it keeps bouncing off the droplets. The early universe was like that — a glowing fog of electrically charged particles that constantly scattered light, so nothing could shine through. Then it cooled enough for those particles to pair up into ordinary atoms, the fog cleared all at once, and the trapped light suddenly flew free in every direction. That freed light is what we now detect as the cosmic microwave background.
depths.core: Before this moment the universe was a 'plasma' — a hot soup where electrons (tiny negative particles) roamed free instead of being attached to atoms. Free electrons are very good at scattering light ('photons'), bouncing them around endlessly, so the universe was 'opaque' (you couldn't see through it). As it expanded and cooled to about 3000 K — at redshift z ≈ 1100, roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang — electrons finally combined with protons to form neutral hydrogen atoms. This event is called 'recombination.' With the free electrons gone, photons stopped scattering and streamed freely; the universe became 'transparent.' The shell of space from which that last-scattered light reaches us is called the 'surface of last scattering,' and the light from it is the cosmic microwave background.
depths.deep: Recombination is not instantaneous — it has finite thickness in redshift, which slightly smears the smallest CMB features; the relevant transition is set by the balance of recombination and ionization (Saha/Peebles equations), and the residual free-electron fraction matters for CMB damping at small scales.

atoms.note: The CMB photons have been traveling freely for ~13.8 billion years, redshifted from ~3000 K to 2.725 K.

quiz.answer: Around z ≈ 1100, about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the temperature fell to ~3000 K.

quiz.prompt: Explain why the universe became transparent at recombination.
quiz.answer: Free electrons (which scatter light) combined with protons into neutral hydrogen, removing the scatterers, so photons could travel freely instead of bouncing around in the plasma.

atoms.title: The cosmic microwave background
atoms.summary: A near-perfect 2.725 K blackbody glow filling the sky — the relic radiation from last scattering.

depths.eli5: Point a sensitive radio antenna anywhere in the sky and you'll pick up a faint, even hum of microwaves coming from every direction. That hum is leftover light from when the universe became see-through, almost 14 billion years ago. It is the oldest light in existence — a baby photo of the entire cosmos.
depths.core: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the light released at recombination, when the universe first became transparent. Since then, expansion has stretched that light enormously, shifting it from a hot glow into the 'microwave' band (the same family of waves as in a microwave oven, but extremely faint) and cooling it to just 2.725 K — only a few degrees above absolute zero. Its 'spectrum' (the brightness at each wavelength) is the most perfect 'blackbody' ever measured in nature — a blackbody being the precise glow that any object in thermal balance gives off — which proves the early universe really was a hot, uniform soup. It was discovered by accident by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson in 1965, and it is the most direct evidence we have of the hot Big Bang.
depths.deep: The CMB is isotropic to about 1 part in 100,000 after removing our motion (the dipole from the Sun's ~370 km/s peculiar velocity); its tiny residual anisotropies encode the initial conditions and contents of the universe, making it cosmology's richest single data set.

atoms.note: COBE (1990s) measured the blackbody spectrum; WMAP and Planck mapped the anisotropies.

quiz.answer: 2.725 K, an almost perfect blackbody (Planck) spectrum.

quiz.prompt: Why is the near-perfect blackbody form of the CMB strong evidence for the hot Big Bang?
quiz.answer: A perfect blackbody requires thermal equilibrium in a hot opaque plasma; only a hot dense early phase could produce it, and expansion preserves the blackbody shape while cooling it.

atoms.title: CMB anisotropies
atoms.summary: Tiny temperature ripples (~1 part in 100,000) across the CMB are the seeds of all cosmic structure.

depths.eli5: The leftover CMB glow looks smooth, but if you measure it incredibly carefully you find it's not perfectly even — there are extremely faint hot spots and cold spots, like very slight mottling. Those spots are a map of the tiny lumps that existed in the baby universe, and those lumps are exactly the seeds that gravity later grew into galaxies and galaxy clusters.
depths.core: 'Anisotropy' just means 'not the same in every direction' — here, tiny differences in the CMB temperature from one patch of sky to another. After subtracting the smooth shift caused by our own motion through space, the temperature varies by only about one part in 100,000 — astonishingly uniform, yet not perfectly so. These variations trace the 'density fluctuations' present at recombination: regions that were slightly denser were slightly hotter and show up as warm spots. Inflation makes specific predictions about the statistical pattern of these spots — they should be 'nearly scale-invariant' (similar strength across sizes), 'Gaussian' (randomly distributed like familiar bell-curve noise), and 'adiabatic' (all components fluctuating together) — and every one of those predictions has been confirmed by satellite measurements.
depths.deep: The anisotropies are decomposed in spherical harmonics into an angular power spectrum C_ℓ; the pattern of correlations at each angular scale encodes the geometry, baryon density, dark matter density, and expansion rate — fitting the C_ℓ curve is how the precise cosmological parameters are extracted.

atoms.art_prompt: a CMB sky map with faint mottled hot and cold spots exaggerated in color, magnified to show the seed density fluctuations

quiz.prompt: How large are the CMB temperature anisotropies relative to the mean temperature?
quiz.answer: About one part in 100,000 (after subtracting the dipole from our motion).

quiz.prompt: What do CMB anisotropies physically correspond to in the early universe?
quiz.answer: Tiny density fluctuations at recombination — slightly denser, hotter regions that later grew gravitationally into galaxies and clusters.

atoms.title: Acoustic peaks and the sound horizon
atoms.summary: Sound waves in the early plasma froze in at recombination, leaving a series of peaks that act as a cosmic ruler.

depths.eli5: Before atoms formed, the universe was a hot soup that could carry sound waves, and it literally rang like a struck bell — but a bell whose tone is frozen in place the instant the universe became transparent. That frozen ringing left a pattern of preferred 'loud' and 'quiet' sizes in the CMB spots. Because we know exactly how far sound could travel before the ringing stopped, that pattern works as a ruler we can hold up to the sky to measure the universe's shape and ingredients.
depths.core: A 'sound wave' is just a pressure ripple traveling through a medium. Before recombination, the push of light ('photon pressure') and the pull of gravity together drove sound waves through the 'baryon–photon plasma' (the soup of ordinary matter and light). The farthest such a wave could travel before recombination froze everything is called the 'sound horizon' — a fixed, known length. When you chart the CMB spots by their angular size (the 'angular power spectrum,' a graph of how much variation appears at each spot-size on the sky), this frozen scale shows up as a series of bumps called 'acoustic peaks.' The angular position of the first peak acts as a 'standard ruler': comparing its known true size to its apparent size on the sky reveals whether space is flat. The relative heights of the peaks weigh how much ordinary matter and dark matter the universe holds.
depths.deep: The first peak sits at ℓ ≈ 220, and its location pins Ω_total ≈ 1 (flat geometry); the ratio of odd to even peak heights reflects baryon loading, and the third-peak height constrains the dark matter density — this is how the CMB delivers percent-level cosmological parameters.

quiz.prompt: What physical scale do the CMB acoustic peaks encode, and what does the first peak's position measure?
quiz.answer: The sound horizon at recombination; the first peak's angular position is a standard ruler that measures spatial curvature (and confirms flatness).

quiz.prompt: Why do the relative heights of the acoustic peaks reveal the baryon density?
quiz.answer: Baryons add inertia to the oscillating plasma, enhancing compression (odd) peaks relative to rarefaction (even) peaks; the odd/even height ratio therefore scales with the baryon density.

atoms.title: Gravitational instability
atoms.summary: Slightly denser regions pull in more matter and grow denser still — gravity amplifies tiny seeds into structure.

depths.eli5: Gravity rewards greed. A patch of space with a little extra matter pulls in nearby matter, which makes it heavier, which makes it pull harder, which makes it heavier still — a runaway snowball effect. Start with the faint lumps recorded in the CMB and let this run for billions of years, and those lumps grow into galaxies and clusters of galaxies.
depths.core: 'Gravitational instability' is the runaway by which small lumps grow into big ones. The tiny density differences imprinted in the CMB ('density fluctuations') are slightly overdense regions; their extra gravity attracts surrounding matter, which raises their 'density contrast' (how much denser they are than average), which strengthens their gravity further. In a static universe this would blow up explosively, but our universe is expanding, and that expansion (the Hubble expansion) constantly pulls matter apart, fighting the collapse. The tug-of-war means the lumps grow only gradually — as a power of the scale factor rather than exponentially — yet over billions of years they amplify enough to assemble all the galaxies and clusters we see.
depths.deep: In the matter-dominated era the density contrast δ grows linearly with the scale factor (δ ∝ a) while perturbations are small; once δ approaches 1 the growth turns nonlinear and regions collapse and virialize — the regime that simulations, not linear theory, must handle.

atoms.art_prompt: a near-uniform field of dots with faint overdensities that progressively pull neighbors in, condensing into clumps over three time steps

quiz.prompt: What process grows tiny density fluctuations into galaxies and clusters?
quiz.answer: Gravitational instability — overdense regions attract more matter and become denser over time.

quiz.prompt: Why do perturbations grow only as a power of the scale factor rather than exponentially in an expanding universe?
quiz.answer: Cosmic expansion dilutes matter and works against collapse, slowing the runaway, so in the matter era the density contrast grows roughly as δ ∝ a.

atoms.title: Evidence for dark matter
atoms.summary: Galaxies rotate too fast, clusters bind too tightly, and lensing is too strong for the visible matter alone.

depths.eli5: Watch the stars at the outer edge of a spinning galaxy. They whirl around so fast that the gravity of everything we can see — all the stars and gas — should not be enough to hold them in; they ought to fly off. They don't. So something we can't see must be there, adding extra gravity. We call that unseen stuff 'dark matter,' and several totally different observations all point to it.
depths.core: 'Dark matter' is matter that gives off no light but still has gravity. Several independent clues all demand far more gravitating mass than the visible stars and gas can supply: (1) 'galaxy rotation curves' — plots of how fast stars orbit versus their distance from the center — stay flat far out, instead of dropping off as visible matter predicts; (2) galaxies inside clusters zip around too fast to stay bound by visible mass alone; (3) 'gravitational lensing' (the bending of light by mass) is stronger than the visible matter can account for; and (4) the heights of the CMB acoustic peaks require it. All four converge on an unseen, 'non-baryonic' component (not made of ordinary protons and neutrons) about five times more abundant than ordinary matter.
depths.deep: The Bullet Cluster is a striking case: in a cluster collision the hot gas (most of the baryons) lags behind while the lensing mass tracks the galaxies, spatially separating the bulk of the mass from the bulk of the baryons — hard to explain by modifying gravity alone.

atoms.art_prompt: a galaxy rotation curve staying flat far beyond the visible disk, beside a Bullet-Cluster image with lensing mass offset from the X-ray gas

quiz.prompt: Give two independent lines of evidence for dark matter.
quiz.answer: Flat galaxy rotation curves and gravitational lensing / cluster dynamics that exceed what visible matter can explain (also the CMB peak heights).

quiz.prompt: Why does the Bullet Cluster favor dark matter over modified gravity?
quiz.answer: The lensing mass is spatially offset from the dominant baryonic component (the hot gas), so the gravitating mass is not where most of the ordinary matter is.

atoms.title: Dark matter halos
atoms.summary: Dark matter collapses first into extended halos; galaxies form as gas falls into these gravitational wells.

depths.eli5: Invisible dark matter clumps together into big roughly-round blobs first. Later, ordinary gas drains down into the middle of each blob — like water collecting in a bowl — and that gas lights up into the stars and galaxies we can actually see. So every glowing galaxy sits at the heart of a much bigger, invisible blob.
depths.core: A 'halo' here is a large, roughly spherical cloud of dark matter surrounding a galaxy. Dark matter clumps before ordinary matter does, and the reason is subtle: before recombination, ordinary matter ('baryons') was held smooth by the constant push of light ('radiation pressure'), but dark matter ignores light entirely, so it was free to start collapsing earlier. These early dark-matter clumps form 'potential wells' — gravitational valleys. Ordinary gas then falls into those valleys, cools off by radiating away energy as light, and condenses into stars and galaxies at the bottom. The visible galaxy is therefore just the bright tip embedded in a far larger, more massive dark matter halo that supplies most of the gravity.
depths.deep: N-body simulations of cold dark matter produce halos with a near-universal density profile (the NFW form) and a hierarchical merger history — small halos form first and merge into larger ones, a prediction that broadly matches observed galaxy clustering.

atoms.art_prompt: a glowing galaxy nested at the center of a large translucent spherical dark-matter halo, with gas streaming inward to form stars

quiz.prompt: Why does dark matter begin collapsing into halos before ordinary matter?
quiz.answer: It does not feel radiation pressure, so it can start clumping while baryons are still held smooth by photons before recombination.

quiz.prompt: Explain how galaxies relate to dark matter halos.
quiz.answer: Galaxies form when gas falls into pre-existing dark matter halos, cools, and condenses into stars; the visible galaxy sits at the center of a much larger, more massive dark halo.

atoms.title: Large-scale structure
atoms.summary: Galaxies trace a cosmic web of filaments, walls, and voids — the largest patterns gravity has built.

depths.eli5: If you map out where all the galaxies are, they don't fill space evenly like sprinkles in batter. Instead they string themselves into glowing threads that wrap around gigantic nearly-empty bubbles — a pattern that looks strikingly like a spiderweb or a sponge. This 'cosmic web' is the biggest structure gravity has ever built.
depths.core: 'Large-scale structure' is the overall arrangement of galaxies across the universe. By measuring millions of galaxy positions ('redshift surveys' — see the redshift-survey atom), astronomers find galaxies organized into a 'cosmic web': long 'filaments' (threads) and 'sheets' (walls) of galaxies surrounding huge nearly-empty regions called 'voids,' with dense clusters of galaxies sitting where the filaments cross. This web is the grown-up result of gravitational instability acting on the faint seeds seen in the CMB. Statisticians describe it with tools like the 'two-point correlation function' (how much more likely two galaxies are to sit a given distance apart than by chance) and the 'power spectrum' (how clustering strength varies with size); both encode the matter density and the nature of dark matter.
depths.deep: Cold dark matter predicts this web in detail; the observed clustering (including the baryon acoustic oscillation feature at ~150 Mpc) matches simulations, while a hot (fast-moving) dark matter would have erased small-scale structure — a key reason dark matter is believed to be 'cold'.

atoms.art_prompt: a 3D redshift-survey slice showing galaxies strung along filaments around dark voids, clusters glowing at the nodes of the cosmic web

quiz.prompt: What overall pattern do galaxies form on the largest scales?
quiz.answer: A cosmic web of filaments and sheets around large voids, with clusters at the intersections.

quiz.prompt: Why does the existence of fine-grained cosmic-web structure argue for COLD rather than hot dark matter?
quiz.answer: Fast-moving (hot) dark matter would free-stream out of small overdensities and wash out small-scale structure; the observed sharp structure requires slow-moving (cold) dark matter.

atoms.title: Baryon acoustic oscillations
atoms.summary: The same early sound waves left a ~150 Mpc preferred separation between galaxies — a standard ruler in 3D.

depths.eli5: Remember the early universe rang like a bell (the acoustic-peaks atom)? That same ringing left a subtle fingerprint in where galaxies ended up: pairs of galaxies are very slightly more likely to sit about 500 million light-years apart than any other distance. Because that special separation is a fixed, known length, astronomers use it as a giant tape measure to gauge distances and track how the universe has expanded.
depths.core: The same sound waves that left the acoustic peaks in the CMB also stamped a faint preferred distance into the arrangement of matter: galaxies are slightly more likely to be separated by the 'sound horizon,' about 150 megaparsecs ('comoving,' meaning measured in today's stretched-out units; that's roughly 500 million light-years). This shows up as a small bump in the 'galaxy correlation function' (the graph of how galaxy-pair counts depend on separation). Because the true length of this 'baryon acoustic oscillation' (BAO) feature is known, it serves as a 'standard ruler': by measuring how big it appears at different redshifts (different cosmic eras), astronomers chart the expansion history of the universe.
depths.deep: Because the BAO scale is set by early-universe physics measurable from the CMB, it is a 'calibrated' ruler; comparing its apparent size across redshift constrains H(z) and the dark energy equation of state largely independently of the supernova distance ladder.

quiz.prompt: What is the approximate comoving scale of the baryon acoustic oscillation feature?
quiz.answer: About 150 megaparsecs — the sound horizon at recombination imprinted on the galaxy distribution.

quiz.prompt: Why is BAO called a 'standard ruler' and how is it used?
quiz.answer: Its physical length is fixed and calibrated by the CMB; measuring its apparent angular/redshift size at different epochs maps the expansion history H(z).

atoms.title: Standard candles
atoms.summary: Objects of known intrinsic brightness let you read distance from how dim they appear.

depths.eli5: If two identical light bulbs are in front of you and one looks dimmer, you instantly know it's farther away. Astronomers use the same trick: if they know how bright an object truly is, they can judge its distance from how bright it merely appears. Certain stars and certain stellar explosions are dependable cosmic 'light bulbs' of known true brightness.
depths.core: A 'standard candle' is any object whose real, intrinsic brightness ('luminosity') is known in advance. Compare that to how bright it looks from Earth and the distance falls out of the 'inverse-square law' — the rule that brightness fades as 1 divided by distance squared (twice as far looks four times dimmer). Two workhorses fill different distance ranges: 'Cepheid variable stars' pulse in size and brightness, and the speed of their pulsing reliably reveals their luminosity, which calibrates distances to nearby galaxies; and 'Type Ia supernovae' — runaway thermonuclear explosions of white-dwarf stars that all peak at nearly the same brightness — are bright enough to be seen billions of light-years away, extending the measurement of the universe's expansion to enormous distances.
depths.deep: The distance ladder is built in rungs (parallax → Cepheids → Type Ia SNe), and each rung's calibration error propagates; Type Ia luminosity is standardized using the light-curve shape (brighter supernovae decline more slowly), without which they would not be precise enough for cosmology.

atoms.note: Type Ia supernovae as standard candles drove the 1998 discovery of accelerating expansion.
atoms.art_prompt: a distance ladder with rungs labeled parallax, Cepheids, and Type Ia supernovae, each reaching farther into a field of galaxies

quiz.prompt: What property of a standard candle lets it measure distance?
quiz.answer: Its known intrinsic luminosity — comparing it to the observed brightness gives distance via the inverse-square law.

quiz.prompt: Why are Type Ia supernovae especially valuable as standard candles?
quiz.answer: They have nearly uniform (and light-curve-standardizable) peak brightness and are extremely luminous, so they can be seen across cosmological distances to trace the expansion history.

atoms.title: Redshift surveys and cosmic mapping
atoms.summary: Measuring millions of galaxy redshifts converts the sky into a 3D map of the universe.

depths.eli5: We already know a galaxy's redshift tells us roughly how far away it is. Now do that for millions of galaxies across the sky, and you can place each one at its proper depth — turning a flat picture of dots into a real three-dimensional map of the universe, showing where the threads and empty bubbles of the cosmic web actually are.
depths.core: A 'redshift survey' is a project that records the 'spectrum' (the rainbow breakdown of light) of huge numbers of galaxies. Each spectrum reveals that galaxy's redshift, which converts to a distance, so the survey can plot every galaxy in three dimensions. Surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) have mapped millions of galaxies this way. The resulting 3D maps reveal the cosmic web directly and let cosmologists extract statistical measurements — the 'galaxy power spectrum' (how strongly galaxies clump at each size scale), the correlation function, and the BAO standard-ruler scale — that pin down what the universe is made of and what shape it has.
depths.deep: Redshift maps are distorted by galaxies' peculiar velocities ('redshift-space distortions'): infall toward overdensities squashes structures along the line of sight, an effect that, rather than being mere noise, measures the growth rate of structure and tests gravity on cosmic scales.

atoms.art_prompt: a wedge diagram of a galaxy redshift survey fanning out from Earth, each galaxy placed by its redshift, revealing filaments and voids

quiz.prompt: What quantity does a redshift survey use to estimate each galaxy's distance?
quiz.answer: The galaxy's redshift, converted to distance via the Hubble law / FRW relation.

quiz.prompt: What are redshift-space distortions and why are they useful rather than just a nuisance?
quiz.answer: Peculiar velocities shift apparent positions along the line of sight; this distortion measures the growth rate of structure and tests gravity on large scales.

atoms.title: Dark energy and accelerating expansion
atoms.summary: Distant supernovae revealed that cosmic expansion is speeding up, driven by a repulsive 'dark energy'.

depths.eli5: You'd expect gravity to be slowly putting the brakes on the universe's expansion — everything pulling on everything else. The shock of 1998 was the opposite: the expansion is actually speeding up. Something invisible is acting like an anti-gravity, pushing space apart, and we call it 'dark energy.'
depths.core: In 1998 two rival teams measured distant Type Ia supernovae (the standard-candle explosions) and found them dimmer — and therefore farther away — than a slowing-down universe should allow. That meant the expansion is 'accelerating' (speeding up). In the Friedmann equations, speeding up requires an ingredient with strongly 'negative pressure' (pressure that pulls inward, here about p ≈ −ρc², where ρ is its energy density and c is the speed of light) — which, counterintuitively, drives space apart on the largest scales. This 'dark energy' makes up roughly 70% of the total energy of the universe and dominates the cosmos today, even though no one yet knows what it actually is.
depths.deep: Acceleration follows from the second Friedmann equation, ä/a ∝ −(ρ + 3p/c²): any component with p < −ρc²/3 pushes ä > 0. Whether dark energy is a constant Λ or evolves (an equation-of-state parameter w possibly ≠ −1) is a central observational question.

atoms.note: The 1998 discovery won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics (Perlmutter, Schmidt, Riess).

atoms.title: Cosmological constant Λ
atoms.summary: The simplest dark energy is a constant vacuum energy density — Einstein's Λ, restored to explain acceleration.

depths.eli5: Here's the simplest possible explanation for dark energy: empty space itself carries a fixed amount of energy that never thins out, no matter how much the universe grows. Ordinary matter spreads thinner as space expands, but this energy-of-empty-space stays the same density forever — so as everything else fades, its steady outward push eventually wins and the expansion speeds up.
depths.core: The 'cosmological constant,' written Λ (the Greek letter lambda), is the extra term Einstein once added to his field equations. Treated as dark energy, it behaves like a uniform energy density built into empty space (the 'vacuum') that stays exactly constant over time and has negative pressure. Its 'equation of state' — the ratio of pressure to energy density, labeled w — equals −1, the hallmark of a true constant. Because matter and radiation dilute as the universe expands while Λ does not, Λ inevitably overtakes them and comes to dominate, producing accelerating expansion. It is the simplest dark-energy model and fits current data well, which is why it's the 'Λ' in the standard ΛCDM model.
depths.deep: Identifying Λ with quantum vacuum energy yields a prediction off by ~120 orders of magnitude from the observed value — the 'cosmological constant problem,' one of the deepest unsolved puzzles in physics, plus the 'coincidence problem' of why Λ and matter densities are comparable right now.

quiz.prompt: What is the equation-of-state parameter w for a cosmological constant?
quiz.answer: w = −1: pressure equals minus the energy density, p = −ρc².

quiz.prompt: Why does the cosmological constant inevitably come to dominate the universe over time?
quiz.answer: Its energy density stays constant while matter and radiation densities dilute as the universe expands, so eventually Λ outweighs everything else.

atoms.title: ΛCDM — the standard model of cosmology
atoms.summary: A flat universe of ~5% atoms, ~27% cold dark matter, ~68% dark energy fits nearly all cosmological data.

depths.eli5: Cosmology's grand summary is one short recipe for the whole universe: a pinch of ordinary matter (atoms), a big helping of invisible cold dark matter, and an even bigger helping of dark energy, all in a flat universe that got its start from inflation. Remarkably, that single recipe with just a handful of dials explains almost every cosmic observation at once.
depths.core: ΛCDM (say 'Lambda-C-D-M') is the 'standard model of cosmology,' also called the 'concordance model' because many independent datasets agree on it. The name spells out its two key ingredients: Λ (the cosmological constant, i.e. dark energy) and CDM ('cold dark matter' — dark matter that moves slowly, which is what lets fine structure form). It describes a spatially flat universe whose lumps were seeded by inflation's nearly even fluctuations. The mix is roughly 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, and 68% dark energy. With only about six adjustable numbers ('free parameters'), this one model simultaneously fits the CMB, the large-scale galaxy web, Big Bang nucleosynthesis, and supernova distances — an extraordinary feat of economy.
depths.deep: Its economy is its strength: six parameters fit thousands of CMB multipoles and galaxy statistics. Yet it is descriptive, not explanatory — it names dark matter and dark energy without identifying them, and emerging tensions (notably in H₀) probe whether it is complete.

atoms.note: Often called the 'concordance model' because independent data sets agree on its parameters.

atoms.title: The cosmic distance ladder
atoms.summary: Distances are bootstrapped in rungs — parallax to Cepheids to supernovae — each calibrating the next.

depths.eli5: No single tool can measure every cosmic distance, so astronomers climb a ladder. The bottom rung measures nearby stars directly; that result calibrates a tool good for slightly farther objects; that one calibrates a tool for even farther objects; and so on out to distant galaxies. Each rung leans on the rung beneath it — which is why the whole thing is called a 'ladder.'
depths.core: The 'cosmic distance ladder' is the chain of methods astronomers use to measure ever-greater distances, each one calibrating the next. The bottom rung is 'parallax,' a pure geometry trick: a nearby star appears to shift slightly against the background as Earth orbits the Sun, and the size of that shift gives the distance directly. Parallax distances calibrate Cepheid variable stars; Cepheids (visible in nearby galaxies) in turn calibrate Type Ia supernovae; and supernovae, bright enough to see across the cosmos, reach the far universe. Combine the ladder's distances with the galaxies' redshifts and you get the Hubble constant and the history of cosmic expansion.
depths.deep: Each rung inherits the calibration uncertainty of the rungs below, so systematic errors (e.g., Cepheid metallicity, dust, supernova standardization) propagate up the ladder — which is exactly where the local-distance-ladder value of H₀ might diverge from the early-universe value.

quiz.prompt: Name the three classic rungs of the cosmic distance ladder in order of increasing reach.
quiz.answer: Geometric parallax, Cepheid variable stars, and Type Ia supernovae.

quiz.prompt: Why does a calibration error in one rung threaten the whole ladder?
quiz.answer: Each rung is calibrated by the one below it, so a systematic error propagates upward and biases the final distance and H₀ estimate.

atoms.title: Horizons and the observable universe
atoms.summary: Light has only had finite time to reach us, so we see a sphere ~46 billion light-years in comoving radius.

depths.eli5: Light travels fast but not instantly, and the universe is only so old. So we can only see things whose light has had time to reach us since the beginning. That sets an edge to what we can observe — not an edge of the universe itself, just an edge of our view. Beyond it the universe almost certainly keeps going; its light simply hasn't arrived yet.
depths.core: Because the universe has a finite age (about 13.8 billion years), light has only had so long to travel, which creates a 'particle horizon' — the greatest distance from which light could possibly have reached us by now. The 'observable universe' is everything inside that horizon. Its present 'comoving radius' (distance measured in today's stretched-out units) is about 46 billion light-years. That's far bigger than the naive 13.8 billion light-years you'd guess from the age, because space kept expanding while the ancient light was in transit, carrying its sources much farther away. The whole universe is at least this big and probably vastly larger — we just can't see past our horizon.
depths.deep: There is also a cosmological event horizon in an accelerating universe: galaxies beyond a certain comoving distance are receding such that their future light will never reach us, so the observable universe's content (not just its apparent edge) is being slowly cut off as Λ dominates.

quiz.prompt: Roughly what is the comoving radius of the observable universe?
quiz.answer: About 46 billion light-years, even though the universe is only ~13.8 billion years old.

quiz.prompt: Why is the observable universe larger than 13.8 billion light-years despite light only traveling for 13.8 billion years?
quiz.answer: Space expanded while the light was in transit, so the regions that emitted ancient light are now much farther away than the distance the light covered.

atoms.title: Gravitational lensing
atoms.summary: Mass bends light, so foreground masses magnify and distort background galaxies — a direct probe of total mass.

depths.eli5: Just as a glass lens bends light to form an image, a heavy object in space bends the light passing near it. So when a massive galaxy or galaxy cluster sits between us and something farther away, it warps and magnifies the background object's light. By studying exactly how that light gets bent, astronomers can weigh the foreground mass — including mass we can't see at all.
depths.core: General relativity predicts that mass bends the path of light (recall spacetime curvature steering everything that moves, including light). A foreground galaxy or cluster therefore acts as a 'gravitational lens,' producing stretched 'arcs,' multiple copies of a single background source, and overall magnification. The crucial point: lensing responds to ALL mass — whether it shines or not — so it maps the total mass directly, making it one of the best tools for detecting dark matter and measuring the geometry of the universe. 'Strong lensing' gives dramatic, obvious arcs and even complete 'Einstein rings'; 'weak lensing' is far subtler, a roughly 1% systematic warping of the shapes of millions of galaxies ('cosmic shear') that only shows up statistically.
depths.deep: Strong lensing makes dramatic arcs and Einstein rings; weak lensing measures subtle ~1% shape distortions of millions of galaxies statistically ('cosmic shear'), probing the growth of structure and constraining the matter density and dark energy independently of galaxy bias.

atoms.note: First confirmed in 1919 (light bending by the Sun during a solar eclipse) — an early triumph of general relativity.

quiz.prompt: What does gravitational lensing respond to that makes it valuable for dark matter studies?
quiz.answer: Total mass — both luminous and dark — so it maps mass directly regardless of whether it emits light.

quiz.prompt: Distinguish strong from weak gravitational lensing.
quiz.answer: Strong lensing produces visible arcs, multiple images, and Einstein rings; weak lensing produces tiny statistical shape distortions ('cosmic shear') measured over many galaxies.

atoms.title: The Hubble tension
atoms.summary: Local and early-universe measurements of H₀ disagree at ~5σ — possibly a crack in ΛCDM.

depths.eli5: Two trustworthy methods both try to measure how fast the universe is expanding today, and they keep getting different answers. The gap is now too big to blame on bad luck or sloppy measuring. So either there's a subtle mistake nobody has spotted, or our theory of the universe is missing something. This unsolved disagreement is the 'Hubble tension.'
depths.core: Both numbers are values of the Hubble constant H₀, the expansion rate today. The 'distance-ladder' method (climb parallax → Cepheids → Type Ia supernovae, as in the SH0ES project) measures the nearby universe directly and gets H₀ ≈ 73 km/s/Mpc. The 'early-universe' method instead reads H₀ off the Planck satellite's CMB map by assuming the ΛCDM model, and gets ≈ 67.4 km/s/Mpc. The gap between them is about '5σ' — '5 sigma' means five times the size of the expected measurement scatter, a level physicists treat as far too large to be random chance. So this is a real puzzle: it points to either an undiscovered measurement error ('systematic') or a genuine gap in ΛCDM.
depths.deep: Independent BAO+BBN inferences cluster near the low (Planck) value, sharpening the puzzle; proposed fixes like early dark energy modify the sound horizon before recombination, but no single model yet resolves H₀ without worsening other data — the tension remains genuinely open.

atoms.title: Is dark energy evolving?
atoms.summary: Whether dark energy is a constant Λ (w = −1) or evolves with time is a central open question.

depths.eli5: Is dark energy a fixed, unchanging feature of empty space, steady for all time? Or is it a slowly shifting something that was different in the past and may change in the future? Right now we can't be sure — and figuring out which it is would be a huge clue to what dark energy actually is.
depths.core: The 'equation of state' of dark energy is captured by a single number w — the ratio of its pressure to its energy density. A true cosmological constant (the Λ in ΛCDM) has w exactly equal to −1, fixed forever. But dark energy might instead be a 'dynamical field' (an evolving kind of energy spread through space) whose w isn't −1, or whose w drifts over time. Big surveys that combine supernovae, baryon acoustic oscillations, and weak gravitational lensing are trying to pin w down precisely. Any solid, reproducible departure from w = −1 would rule out the simple constant and force new physics into the picture.
depths.deep: Recent BAO datasets have hinted at mild evidence for evolving dark energy (w₀–wₐ parametrizations preferred over constant Λ at modest significance), but the result is sensitive to data combinations and systematics — a live, unsettled debate rather than a confirmed discovery.

quiz.answer: w = −1 exactly is a cosmological constant; any robust deviation or time-variation in w indicates dynamical dark energy.

quiz.answer: It would rule out a simple constant vacuum energy and require dark energy to be a dynamical entity, pointing to new physics beyond ΛCDM.

atoms.title: Primordial gravitational waves (B-modes)
atoms.summary: Inflation should have produced gravitational waves imprinting a faint curl pattern (B-modes) in the CMB polarization.

depths.eli5: If inflation really happened, that violent burst of expansion would have rippled spacetime itself, sending out 'gravitational waves' — stretching-and-squeezing ripples in space. Those ripples would leave a faint, twisty swirl pattern in the way the CMB's light is oriented. Finding that swirl would be a smoking gun for inflation, and teams are hunting hard for it.
depths.core: 'Gravitational waves' are ripples in spacetime that travel outward when mass-energy is violently rearranged; inflation should have produced a faint background of 'primordial' ones from the universe's first instant. Their strength is summarized by the 'tensor-to-scalar ratio' r (how big the gravitational-wave ripples are compared to the ordinary density ripples), and r encodes the energy scale at which inflation happened. Light can be 'polarized' (its waves preferentially oriented one way), and these primordial gravitational waves would stamp a special curl-shaped, swirl-like polarization pattern on the CMB called 'B-mode' polarization (as opposed to the simpler gradient-shaped 'E-mode'). Detecting primordial B-modes would be powerful evidence for inflation and a window onto physics at energies far beyond any particle accelerator.
depths.deep: Primordial B-modes have not been detected; current limits (r < ~0.03) already exclude some inflation models, and the search is confounded by galactic foreground B-modes from dust — the lesson of the 2014 BICEP2 episode, where a claimed detection was reattributed to foreground dust.

atoms.note: A confirmed primordial B-mode signal would be among the most important discoveries in physics.
